questions.question: Abnormal increase in blood volume is called: a). Hypovolemia b). Hypervolemia c). Hemodilution d). Polycythemia
questions.solution_html:
• b) Hypervolemia
  • Deficiency of calcitriol resulting in reduction of calcium absorption from intestine and
  • hypocalcemia. Deficiency of calcitriol and hypocalcemia may cause secondary
  • hyperparathyroidism in some patients
  • Proximal Convoluted Tubule or PCT or Pars Convoluta
  • ● It is about 14 mm long. It forms about 1/3rd of renal tubules. It is lined by large
  • columnar (cuboidal) cells having brush borders or microvilli which are prolongations of
  • cytoplasm.
  • ● It increases the surface area for absorption. Tubular invaginations to cytoplasm
  • between microvilli are called apical canaliculi which help in protein absorption.
  • ● 60-80% of sodium, chloride and water entering the PCT are reabsorbed here.
  • ● The rate of reabsorption is directly proportional to GFR.

questions.final_answer: ● The rate of reabsorption is directly proportional to GFR.

questions.question: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of human respiratory system and describe its structure.
questions.solution_html:
• ● Diagram – (1 mark)
  • ● Each nephron is formed by two parts
  • a) A blind end called renal corpuscle or Malpighian corpuscle
  • b) A tubular portion called renal tubule. (1/2 mark)
  • a) RENAL CORPUSCLE (1/4 mark each (1 marks))
  • ● Renal corpuscle or Malpighian corpuscle is a spheroidal and slightly flattened
  • structure with a diameter of about 200 µ.
  • ● It is situated in the cortex of the kidney either near the periphery or near the medulla.
  • ● Function of the renal corpuscle is the filtration of blood which forms the first phase of
  • urine formation.
  • ● It has two parts: glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule
  • ● i) Glomerulus (1/4 mark each – 1 1/2 marks)
  • ● Glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries enclosed by Bowman capsule. It consists of
  • glomerular capillaries interposed between afferent arteriole on one end and efferent
  • arteriole on the other end.
  • ● Glomerular capillaries arise from the afferent arteriole. After entering the Bowman
  • capsule, the afferent arteriole divides into 4 or 5 large capillaries.
  • ● Each large capillary subdivides into many small capillaries. These small capillaries
  • are arranged in irregular loops. All the smaller capillaries finally reunite to form the
  • efferent arteriole, which leaves the Bowman capsule.
  • ● The afferent vessel is short and wide whereas the efferent arteriole is narrow and long.
  • These arrangements make the glomerular B.P much higher and facilitate filtration.
  • ● Glomerular capillaries are made up of single layer of endothelial cells, which are
  • attached to a basement membrane.
  • ● Endothelium has many pores called fenestrae or filtration pores. These pores helps in
  • the filtration process.
  • ii) Bowman’s Capsule (2 marks – ¼ mark for each point)
  • ● Bowman’s capsule consists of inner visceral layer surrounding the glomerulus and
  • outer parietal layer bordering the renal corpuscle.
  • ● Between these two layers is urinary space where the primary urine is produced.
  • ● Epithelial cells of the visceral layer fuse with the basement membrane but the fusion
  • is not complete.
  • ● Each cell is connected with basement membrane by cytoplasmic extensions of
  • epithelial cells called pedicles or feet.
  • ● Epithelial cells with pedicles are called podocytes.
  • ● The pedicles are arranged in an interdigitating manner leaving small cleft-like spaces
  • in between.
  • ● The cleft like space is called slit pore.
  • ● These filtration slits are components of filtration barrier for for ultrafiltration of blood
  • plasma and thus for primary urine production.
  • b) RENAL TUBULE (4 marks – ¼ mark for each point)
questions.final_answer: b) RENAL TUBULE  – ¼ mark for each point)

questions.question: is the process of forming clots in the wall of an injured blood vessels and preventing blood loss. A) Hemostasis B) Homeostasis C) Coagulation D) Vasoconstriction
questions.solution_html:
• Hemostasis & stages
  • Hemostasis is the process of stopping bleeding by forming a clot at the site of blood vessel
  • injury(.1 mark) Stages of Hemostasis
  • i. Vasoconstriction (2marks)
  • Immediate constriction of injured blood vessels to reduce blood loss; mediated by substances
  • like serotonin released from platelets.
  • ii. Platelet Plug Formation(2marks)
  • Platelets adhere to exposed collagen, get activated, and aggregate to form a temporary plug
  • at the injury site.
  • iii. Coagulation (Blood Clotting) – Steps(5 marks)
  • ● Formation of Prothrombin Activator- Formed by intrinsic (within blood) and extrinsic
  • (tissue injury) pathways.
  • ● Prothrombin → Thrombin- Prothrombin is converted into thrombin in the presence of
  • calcium.
  • ● Fibrinogen → Fibrin- Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin threads.
  • ● Clot Formation- Fibrin threads form a mesh over platelet plug to create a stable clot.
  • ● Clot Stabilization- Factor XIII strengthens fibrin to make the clot firm and permanent.
questions.final_answer: ● Clot Stabilization- Factor XIII strengthens fibrin to make the clot firm and permanent.

questions.question: Bile is produced by the: a). Gall bladder b). Pancreas c). Liver d). Small intestine
questions.solution_html:
• ● Systolic Heart Failure - the heart failure due to the decreased ability of heart to contract.
  • It is caused either by muscular weakness or valvular defect. Ventricles may be filled with
  • blood but cannot pump it out with sufficient force. As a result, more amount of blood
  • remains in ventricle, accumulating in lungs or systemic veins or both. (2 marks)
  • ● Diastolic Heart Failure - the heart failure that occurs when the ventricles cannot relax
  • properly due to the stiffening of cardiac muscle. So, there is reduction in ventricular filling
  • and cardiac output. (1 mark)
  • ● Right sided heart failure - occurs due to loss of pumping action of the right side of the
  • heart. So, blood accumulates in right atrium and blood vessels. It causes edema in the feet
  • ankles, legs and abdomen. (1 mark)
  • ● Left Sided Heart Failure - due to the loss of pumping action of the left side of the heart.
  • It causes congestion of lungs. (1 mark)
  • Essay

questions.question: Explain structure of kidney with a neat diagram.
questions.solution_html:
• ● Diagram – (1 mark)
  • ● Each nephron is formed by two parts
  • a) A blind end called renal corpuscle or Malpighian corpuscle
  • b) A tubular portion called renal tubule. (1/2 mark)
  • a) RENAL CORPUSCLE (1/4 mark each (1 marks))
  • ● Renal corpuscle or Malpighian corpuscle is a spheroidal and slightly flattened
  • structure with a diameter of about 200 µ.
  • ● It is situated in the cortex of the kidney either near the periphery or near the medulla.
  • ● Function of the renal corpuscle is the filtration of blood which forms the first phase of
  • urine formation.
  • ● It has two parts: glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule
  • ● i) Glomerulus (1/4 mark each – 1 1/2 marks)
  • ● Glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries enclosed by Bowman capsule. It consists of
  • glomerular capillaries interposed between afferent arteriole on one end and efferent
  • arteriole on the other end.
  • ● Glomerular capillaries arise from the afferent arteriole. After entering the Bowman
  • capsule, the afferent arteriole divides into 4 or 5 large capillaries.
  • ● Each large capillary subdivides into many small capillaries. These small capillaries
  • are arranged in irregular loops. All the smaller capillaries finally reunite to form the
  • efferent arteriole, which leaves the Bowman capsule.
  • ● The afferent vessel is short and wide whereas the efferent arteriole is narrow and long.

  • attached to a basement membrane.

  • in between.
  • ● The cleft like space is called slit pore.
  • ● These filtration slits are components of filtration barrier for for ultrafiltration of blood
  • plasma and thus for primary urine production.

questions.question: Explain heart failure on the basis of side of heart affected. Part D Essay
questions.solution_html:
• ● Systolic Heart Failure - the heart failure due to the decreased ability of heart to contract.
  • It is caused either by muscular weakness or valvular defect. Ventricles may be filled with
  • blood but cannot pump it out with sufficient force. As a result, more amount of blood
  • remains in ventricle, accumulating in lungs or systemic veins or both. (2 marks)
  • ● Diastolic Heart Failure - the heart failure that occurs when the ventricles cannot relax
  • properly due to the stiffening of cardiac muscle. So, there is reduction in ventricular filling
  • and cardiac output. (1 mark)
  • ● Right sided heart failure - occurs due to loss of pumping action of the right side of the
  • heart. So, blood accumulates in right atrium and blood vessels. It causes edema in the feet
  • ankles, legs and abdomen. (1 mark)
  • ● Left Sided Heart Failure - due to the loss of pumping action of the left side of the heart.
  • It causes congestion of lungs. (1 mark)
  • Essay

questions.question: Define hemostasis and enumerate the stages involved in prevention of blood loss.
questions.solution_html:
• Hemostasis & stages
  • Hemostasis is the process of stopping bleeding by forming a clot at the site of blood vessel
  • injury(.1 mark) Stages of Hemostasis
  • i. Vasoconstriction (2marks)
  • Immediate constriction of injured blood vessels to reduce blood loss; mediated by substances
  • like serotonin released from platelets.
  • ii. Platelet Plug Formation(2marks)
  • Platelets adhere to exposed collagen, get activated, and aggregate to form a temporary plug
  • at the injury site.
  • iii. Coagulation (Blood Clotting) – Steps(5 marks)
  • ● Formation of Prothrombin Activator- Formed by intrinsic (within blood) and extrinsic
  • (tissue injury) pathways.
  • ● Prothrombin → Thrombin- Prothrombin is converted into thrombin in the presence of
  • calcium.
  • ● Fibrinogen → Fibrin- Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin threads.
  • ● Clot Formation- Fibrin threads form a mesh over platelet plug to create a stable clot.
  • ● Clot Stabilization- Factor XIII strengthens fibrin to make the clot firm and permanent.

questions.question: Explain iron distribution, absorption, transport and storage in our body.
questions.solution_html:
• Distribution of Iron in the Body
  • Dietary Iron
  • Dietary iron is available in two forms called heme and non-heme. (1 mark)
  • ● Heme iron – It is present in fish, meat and chicken. Iron in these sources is found in
  • the form of heme. Heme iron is absorbed easily from intestine. (2 marks)
  • ● Non-heme iron - Iron in the form of non-heme is available in vegetables, grains and
  • cereals. Non-heme iron is not absorbed easily as heme iron. Cereals, flours and
  • products of grains which are enriched or fortified with iron become good dietary
  • sources of non-heme iron, particularly for children and women. (2 marks)
  • Absorption of Iron
  • ● Iron is absorbed mainly from the small intestine.
  • ● It is absorbed through the enterocytes by pinocytosis and transported into the blood.
  • ● Bile is essential for the absorption of iron. Iron is present mostly in ferric (Fe3+)
  • form. It is converted into ferrous form (Fe2+) which is absorbed into the blood.
  • ● Hydrochloric acid from gastric juice makes the ferrous iron soluble so that it could be
  • converted into ferric iron by the enzyme ferric reductase from enterocytes.
  • ● From enterocytes, ferric iron is transported into blood by a protein called ferroportin.
  • ● In the blood, ferric iron is converted into ferrous iron and transported. ( 3 marks – ½
  • mark for each point)
  • Transport of Iron
  • ● After absorption into blood, iron combines with a β-globulin called apotransferrin
  • resulting in the formation of transferrin.
  • ● Iron is transported in blood in the form of transferrin. Iron combines loosely with
  • globin and can be released easily at any region of the body. ( 1 mark- ½ mark for
  • each point)
  • Storage of Iron
  • ● Iron is stored in large quantities in reticuloendothelial cells and liver hepatocytes
  • ● In the cytoplasm of the cell, iron is stored as ferritin in large amount and Small
  • quantity of iron is also stored as hemosiderin. (1 mark- ½ mark for each point)
